citation: (1) Australian Institute of Company Directors and Human Technology Institute (UTS), A Director's Guide to AI Governance, Version 2, June 2026, https://www.aicd.com.au/content/dam/aicd/pdf/news-media/research/2026/director-guide-to-ai-governance.pdf (opened and text-extracted). (2) ASIC v Bekier (Liability Judgment) [2026] FCA 196, Federal Court of Australia, Lee J, 5 March 2026 (judgment text NOT opened; quoted only as reproduced in the guide and in law-firm commentary).
source_tier: Guide: professional-body and university practitioner guidance (not peer-reviewed). Judgment: primary legal source, but only secondary access achieved. Commentary: law-firm client alerts (Clayton Utz, Ashurst, Maddocks, CSO NSW).
access_status: Guide: fully read via PDF text extraction (relevant passages). Judgment: not opened; only the Lee J extract printed in the guide plus search snippets and web-fetched commentary. NotebookLM summary not seen and not treated as a source.
sponsor_and_incentive: AICD is the professional body for directors and sells membership and training; HTI is a UTS research centre. Guide is advocacy and guidance for boards, not neutral research. Law-firm commentary is marketing to clients.
exact_quotes: Judgment, Lee J, as quoted in the Guide (Part 1, AI use by boards box, near the Telstra example; not independently checked against the judgment): "There is nothing inherently objectionable in obtaining such assistance [from AI], but what ought not occur is that this development becomes an excuse for a failure to instil discipline in the provision of information to directors or leads to a quiet normalisation of private reliance by them upon computer-generated distillations, unregulated by any agreed policy."
Guide, Part 1 (boards' use of AI): "Directors should not rely on AI-generated summaries or analysis as a substitute for their own review and interrogation of board papers."
Guide, same section: "AI tools do not replace the essential human oversight role played by the board and individual directors, nor do they mitigate blind spots or substitute for critical thinking."
Guide, same list: "Directors should take care to ensure the board or individual director use of AI does not undermine confidence in management or blur lines of accountability."
Guide, Ministerial Foreword: "Boards are ultimately accountable for the adoption, implementation and outcomes of AI technologies in their organisations."
Guide, vendor risk section: "While these risks may originate with vendors, accountability remains with the organisation."
Guide's framing sentence: "in ASIC v Bekier (Liability Judgment) [2026] FCA 196, Justice Michael Lee commented on the use of AI in analysing board papers, noting the need for caution."

Via Clayton Utz (secondary, no paragraph number given): AI could address information overload "at least in part" through "the principled and transparent use of emergent technology"; "any use of AI should be controlled and transparent".
date_and_recency: Judgment 5 March 2026. Guide Version 2 June 2026 (AICD page dated 29 June 2026); first edition June 2024. Guide cites a Telstra AFR article dated 23 April 2026.
key_claims: Judgment: former CEO Matthias Bekier and former General Counsel Paula Martin breached s 180(1) Corporations Act care and diligence duties (information not escalated to the board); claims against chairman John O'Neill and the non-executive directors were dismissed (per CSO NSW, DLA Piper, Banco Chambers; secondary). Lee J rejected the argument that reviewing hundreds of pages of board papers was unreasonable (secondary). He commented that AI assistance is not inherently objectionable but must not excuse poor information discipline or lead to unregulated private reliance on AI distillations. Guide: AI tools do not replace directors' own review and critical thinking; boards remain accountable for AI outcomes; use of AI should be governed by policy and not blur accountability.
headline_figures: None quantitative. Only dates and the citation [2026] FCA 196.
sample_unit_and_population: A single Federal Court liability judgment concerning The Star Entertainment Group executives and non-executive directors; a governance guide aimed mainly at ASX300 directors.
observed_vs_stated: Judgment: findings of fact on what executives did and did not escalate; the AI remark is a judicial comment, not a finding on AI use by any party [uncertain: not confirmed whether obiter]. Guide: stated normative guidance, no observed behaviour.
what_makes_trust_justified: Directors personally reviewing and interrogating primary board papers; an agreed policy governing any AI use; transparency and controlled use; AI literacy so directors understand tool strengths and deficiencies; AI registers updated for board use; clear lines of accountability.
what_it_costs: Director time reading full papers (the argument that this was unreasonable was rejected, per commentary); effort to impose discipline on how management supplies information; policy and literacy overhead.
failure_mode_class: Over-reliance on summaries and delegation of judgment; information not escalated (the Star failure was management withholding information, not AI).
control_that_would_have_prevented: Not an AI incident. The Star failures related to escalation to the board and misleading correspondence. Relevant controls for AI: a board AI-use policy, disciplined information provision, and the director's own review of source papers.
limitations_stated: Guide states that "the legal and regulatory boundaries are still blurry" and that boards will need to exercise judgements about adoption. Judgment AI remarks were a comment, not the basis of liability. [uncertain] whether the judgment frames them as obiter.
counter_evidence: Lee J and the guide are not hostile to AI: the judge says there is nothing inherently objectionable, and the guide cites Telstra's in-house board-pack agent as a development. Commentary (Clayton Utz, Maddocks) leans toward AI as a legitimate tool for information overload. The directors who were exonerated were not found to have been negligent for relying on management, so the case is not a ruling against delegation generally [uncertain: reasoning not read].
verification_status: Guide quotes: verified against the opened PDF. Lee J quote: verified only as reproduced in the guide; judgment itself not opened, so paragraph number and context unverified [uncertain]. Case outcome (who was liable): secondary sources only [uncertain]. NotebookLM summary: not available, not a source. Search-summary claims that the duty is 'personal and non-delegable' and that this was the 'first Australian case' on AI in boards come from Clayton Utz/Maddocks and are not verified.
usable_claim: In its June 2026 guide, the AICD and Human Technology Institute say directors should not rely on AI-generated summaries or analysis as a substitute for their own review and interrogation of board papers, and that boards remain ultimately accountable for AI outcomes. The guide quotes Justice Lee in ASIC v Bekier [2026] FCA 196 saying there is nothing inherently objectionable in AI assistance but that it should not become an excuse for poor information discipline or a quiet normalisation of private reliance on computer-generated distillations unregulated by any agreed policy.
do_not_use: Do not say the court held that AI cannot substitute for a director's review, or that the case was decided on AI. The court's liability findings concerned the CEO and General Counsel and escalation to the board. The 'substitute for their own review' wording is the guide's, not the judge's. Do not use the NotebookLM summary. Do not cite paragraph numbers until the judgment is opened.
overlap_with_existing_essays: Not checked against the Verification Gap or Checking Isn't Catching essays in this run; the accountability-cannot-be-delegated theme is likely adjacent.
